While there is still some level of viability in the state, there is very little in the way of contiguous suitable land, and no counties appear to exceed 40% viability. In fact, most counties in Utah do not exceed even 20% viability. The constraints here are primarily logistical in nature. Utah contains portions of both the Wasatch and Uinta Mountain ranges, which preclude large portions of the state due to steep terrain. Much of these lands also have protected status, and include a number of national forests, parks, and monuments, for which the state is quite famous. The other logistical concern is of course that of cooling water. Though the Colorado River does flow through the eastern portion of the state, much of the rest does not have appropriate streamflow resources to support a large light water reactor. Additionally, the state of Utah contains a significant number of active fault lines, though the greatest risk of seismic activity is concentrated along the Wasatch range in the north. This same area also contains one of the few major population centers and areas of open water, both situated around the Great Salt Lake. Utah has two major airports, and several military installations around Tooele and Box Elder counties. All of these considerations amount to a patchwork of suitable regions distributed in a few counties. The story is much the same for the fresh-water cooled SMR configuration, the siting maps for which can be seen in Table U2. This is because the most restrictive criteria do not differ for this configuration. There does however appear to be an increase in viable land for Box Elder, Uintah, and Grand County. For Uintah, this is due to the reduced cooling water requirement, whereas Grand and Box Elder seem to benefit primarily from the relaxed slope constraint. As expected, the removal of the cooling water requirement from the SMR siting maps in Table U3 considerably expands suitability, particularly in the seven counties that flank the western edge of the state. Here still the prevalence of fault lines, steep terrain, and protected regions means that finding contiguous tracts of suitable land will not be a trivial process. In Table U4, the most restrictive criteria are removed for siting data centers, and because of this the vast majority of the state has considerable viability for the technology.
